name: Scheele's Green
lede: Scheele's Green is a yellowish, slightly dulled green named for the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele, who discovered the copper-arsenite pigment behind it in 1775.

sections.title: A bright green chemists learned to fear
sections.body:
Scheele discovered the pigment in Sweden in 1775, though he did not publish his recipe until 1778 [3]. It is a copper arsenite, warm and opaque, and by the end of the nineteenth century it had largely replaced older copper-carbonate greens in paint [3]. It was never adopted widely as an artist's pigment, however, because it discolored in the presence of acid or sulfur fumes and, far more seriously, because it was toxic [3].

The toxicity made Scheele's Green notorious outside the studio [3]. In damp wallpaper, mould growing over the pigment could convert its copper arsenite into trimethylarsine gas, a volatile arsenic compound; families living in rooms papered with it suffered chronic poisoning from their own walls [3]. It fell out of favor after the 1860s as both its toxicity and its instability became impossible to ignore, and was gradually succeeded by other arsenic greens before synthetic, non-toxic pigments replaced the whole family [3].

Ridgway's 1912 atlas lists this exact hue on plate VI, hue 33, tone i, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the name itself to 1778, Scheele's publication year [1]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 68, chroma 44, hue 110, close to [[russet-green|Russet Green]], [[deep-chrysolite-green|Deep Chrysolite Green]] and [[lily-green|Lily Green]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A screen match for this green turns up in 100 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.4 percent, as photographed, concentrated over four times above the archive's average in the 1900s decade [2]. Niels Larsen Stevns, Georges Seurat and Vincent van Gogh all carry it well above the archive's base rate [2]. The earliest dated match in our archive, a 1548 Lucas Cranach portrait, predates Scheele's own discovery by more than two centuries, a reminder that a screen-color match never proves which pigment a painter actually used, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
